promptText: In Java 8+, when a HashMap bucket's collision list grows past a certain threshold, what internal structure does that bucket's linked list convert into to improve worst-case lookup performance?
options: A Red-Black Tree
A second nested HashMap
A skip list
A sorted ArrayList
explanation: Prior to Java 8, colliding entries in a bucket were stored purely as a linked list (O(n) worst case). From Java 8 onward, once a bucket's entry count exceeds the treeify threshold, the list is converted into a Red-Black Tree so lookups degrade to O(log n) instead of O(n).

promptText: What is the key functional difference between Runnable and Callable when submitting work to an ExecutorService, and when should Callable be preferred?
options: Callable can return a value and throw checked exceptions, so it should be preferred when the asynchronous task needs to produce a result
Runnable can throw checked exceptions while Callable cannot, so Runnable is preferred for computations that may fail
Callable always executes synchronously on the calling thread while Runnable is always asynchronous
Runnable only works with newFixedThreadPool while Callable is required for any other pool type
explanation: Runnable's run() returns nothing and cannot declare checked exceptions, while Callable's call() returns a value and can throw checked exceptions. Callable is the natural choice whenever the async task needs to hand back a computed result via a Future.

promptText: A field is declared volatile and multiple threads execute `counter++` on it concurrently. Why is this still not thread-safe?
options: volatile only guarantees visibility of writes across threads, not atomicity, and counter++ is actually a read-modify-write sequence of three separate steps
volatile fields cannot legally be incremented in Java, only directly assigned
volatile silently wraps the field access in a synchronized block, which can deadlock under contention
volatile only applies to object references, so it has no effect on primitive int fields at all
explanation: counter++ decomposes into read, increment, and write. volatile forces each of those individual reads and writes to go to main memory (visibility), but it does nothing to make the three-step sequence atomic, so two threads can still interleave and lose an update.

promptText: What causes the classic N+1 query problem in a JPA/Hibernate application, and what is the standard fix?
options: Lazily fetching a parent's child collection triggers one extra query per parent when the collection is accessed, turning N parents into N additional queries; the fix is to use a join fetch or batch fetching to load children eagerly in fewer round trips
Hibernate always issues exactly N+1 queries for any request regardless of the fetch strategy chosen, and there is no way to avoid it
It only happens when native SQL queries are used instead of JPQL, so switching entirely to JPQL eliminates it
It is a NoSQL-only problem caused by missing secondary indexes, unrelated to relational fetch strategies
explanation: One query loads the N parent rows, then lazy loading fires a separate query per parent to fetch its children, producing N+1 total round trips. Replacing the per-parent lazy fetch with a join fetch or a batched IN-query collapses this back down to a small constant number of queries.

promptText: Why is implementing true, immediate "logout" harder with JWT-based authentication than with traditional server-side sessions?
options: The server never stores the token, so a JWT stays valid until it naturally expires unless extra mechanisms such as a token blocklist or short-lived tokens with refresh rotation are added
JWTs are always persisted in the database, so logging out requires an expensive schema migration
Spring Security cannot parse JWTs at all without an active HTTP session cookie already present
JWT signatures become permanently invalid the instant a user closes their browser tab
explanation: JWT's whole appeal is statelessness: the server does no session lookup and trusts the token's signature and claims. That same property means there is nothing server-side to delete on logout, so genuine revocation requires reintroducing some state, like a blocklist or very short expirations with refresh tokens.

promptText: In the Circuit Breaker resilience pattern, what happens during the HALF_OPEN state?
options: A limited number of trial requests are allowed through to test whether the downstream service has recovered, and the circuit moves back to CLOSED if they succeed
All requests are permanently blocked until an operator manually flips the circuit back to CLOSED
The retry timeout is doubled indefinitely so the failing service is never contacted again
Traffic is silently rerouted to a permanent fallback cache with no further health checking of the primary service
explanation: HALF_OPEN exists specifically to probe recovery without fully reopening the floodgates: a small number of test requests pass through, and success transitions the breaker back to CLOSED while failure sends it back to OPEN.

promptText: A shared static counter is guarded by an instance-level `synchronized` method in one class, while a separate `static synchronized` method in the same class also modifies that counter. Why does this NOT actually prevent race conditions on the counter?
options: Instance and static synchronized methods lock two different monitors (the object instance versus the Class object), so acquiring one never excludes a thread holding the other
Java does not allow the synchronized keyword to be applied to any method that touches a static field
Declaring a method static synchronized automatically makes every field in the class volatile, adding overhead without protection
The JVM silently ignores the synchronized keyword on static methods whenever an instance-level lock already exists elsewhere in the class
explanation: A static synchronized method locks the single Class object shared by all instances, while an instance synchronized method locks that specific object's own monitor. Because these are different locks, mixing the two on the same shared static state is a classic trap: neither excludes the other, so the race condition remains.

promptText: Why does AtomicInteger typically outperform a synchronized counter under moderate thread contention?
options: It relies on a lock-free compare-and-swap loop instead of blocking, avoiding the context-switching and lock-acquisition cost of synchronized
It stores its value in per-thread local storage so no two threads ever contend for the same memory
It disables the JVM's memory visibility guarantees entirely, which makes writes cheaper but riskier
It automatically batches many increments from different threads into a single write via the JIT compiler
explanation: AtomicInteger updates use hardware-level compare-and-swap: a thread reads the current value and retries only if another thread changed it in between, with no thread ever blocked or descheduled. Under very high contention the CAS retries themselves can become wasteful, but for a simple counter it beats synchronized's blocking and context-switch overhead.

promptText: When chaining CompletableFutures, when should thenCompose be used instead of thenApply?
options: When the mapping function itself returns another CompletableFuture, since thenCompose flattens the result instead of producing a nested CompletableFuture<CompletableFuture<T>>
When the continuation must run synchronously on the calling thread rather than on an executor thread
When combining two already-completed, independent futures that have no data dependency on each other
When a checked exception thrown inside the mapping function needs to be converted into a RuntimeException
explanation: thenApply is the CompletableFuture analog of map: it transforms a result in place. thenCompose is the analog of flatMap: it is used when the transformation function itself returns a CompletableFuture, so thenCompose unwraps it into a single flat future rather than leaving a future nested inside a future.

promptText: What is the precise difference between a phantom read and a non-repeatable read in transaction isolation?
options: A phantom read is a query returning a different number of rows on re-execution because another transaction inserted or deleted matching rows, while a non-repeatable read is the same row's values changing because another transaction updated it
Phantom reads only occur under SERIALIZABLE isolation while non-repeatable reads only occur under READ_UNCOMMITTED
Phantom reads are specific to NoSQL databases while non-repeatable reads only apply to relational databases
Non-repeatable reads are caused by dirty writes while phantom reads are caused by another transaction reading uncommitted data
explanation: Non-repeatable read concerns re-reading the same existing row and seeing different column values because a concurrent transaction updated it. Phantom read concerns re-running the same query and getting a different row count because a concurrent transaction inserted or deleted rows that match the query's criteria.

promptText: An order-creation service must guarantee that an audit-log entry is persisted even if the main order transaction later rolls back. Which Spring transaction propagation setting on the audit-logging method achieves this, and why?
options: REQUIRES_NEW, because it suspends the caller's transaction and starts an independent one that can commit on its own regardless of what the caller does afterward
REQUIRED, because joining the existing transaction ensures the audit entry commits or rolls back together with the order for consistency
MANDATORY, because it throws an exception if no transaction exists, which guarantees the audit write is atomic
NESTED, because a savepoint lets the audit write survive independently while still being part of the same physical database transaction
explanation: REQUIRES_NEW suspends any existing transaction and opens a brand-new, independent one for the annotated method. Because the audit write commits in its own transaction, it survives even if the outer order-creation transaction later rolls back — which is exactly the isolation REQUIRED or NESTED cannot provide, since both keep the audit write tied to the outer transaction's fate.

promptText: A developer marks a private method `@Transactional` inside a Spring-managed bean, and also calls another `@Transactional` public method on `this` from within the same class. In both cases, no transaction is ever started. What is the root cause?
options: Spring implements @Transactional via a proxy that only intercepts calls arriving from outside the bean; private methods and self-invoked calls through `this` bypass the proxy entirely, so the transactional advice never runs
@Transactional only takes effect when the method is also annotated with @Async
The Java compiler strips all annotations from private methods during bytecode generation
Spring automatically converts private @Transactional methods to package-private visibility, which disables the AOP weaving plugin
explanation: Spring AOP (proxy-based, not compile-time weaving) wraps the bean in a proxy that intercepts external calls to public methods. A private method can never be proxied, and a call made via `this.someMethod()` from inside the same object also skips the proxy — this is the well-known self-invocation problem, and it affects @Async the same way for the same reason.

promptText: Why can Spring's CGLIB-based AOP proxying not intercept a `final` method, while this specific limitation does not apply the same way to JDK dynamic proxies?
options: CGLIB works by generating a runtime subclass of the target class and overriding its methods to weave in advice, and final methods cannot be overridden; JDK dynamic proxies instead implement the target's interfaces, so they never need to override any concrete class method at all
JDK dynamic proxies use reflection to strip the final modifier from methods at runtime, a trick CGLIB does not support
The Java compiler removes final methods from the compiled bytecode entirely, so neither proxy mechanism can see them, but only CGLIB throws a build error
CGLIB requires every proxied method to first be declared in a Java interface, and interfaces cannot contain final methods
explanation: CGLIB's whole mechanism is subclassing the target class and overriding its methods to insert interception logic — since final methods cannot be overridden by any subclass, CGLIB simply cannot advise them. JDK dynamic proxies sidestep this entirely because they proxy at the interface level, implementing interface methods fresh rather than overriding anything on the concrete class, so a final concrete method is a non-issue as long as it isn't part of the interface being proxied.

promptText: In a classic double-checked-locking singleton, why must the instance field be declared `volatile`?
options: Without volatile, instruction reordering can allow another thread to observe a reference to a partially-constructed object, because the write that publishes the reference and the writes performed by the constructor are not guaranteed to become visible in program order across threads
Without volatile, the JIT compiler refuses to inline the getInstance() method, causing severe performance degradation
Without volatile, the synchronized block inside getInstance() is physically unable to acquire the intrinsic lock
Without volatile, the garbage collector may reclaim the singleton instance between the two null checks
explanation: The Java Memory Model permits the compiler or CPU to reorder the constructor's internal field writes relative to the write that assigns the finished object to the shared reference. Without volatile, a second thread's outer null-check can see a non-null reference whose target object is still mid-construction; volatile establishes the happens-before edge that forbids this reordering, ensuring a fully-initialized object is what other threads observe.

promptText: A team building a simple internal CRUD tool for tracking office supplies is debating adopting CQRS with Event Sourcing "for future-proofing." Based on the tradeoffs of these two patterns, what is the strongest argument against doing so here?
options: Both patterns add genuine complexity — duplicate models, eventual consistency between the write and read sides, and replay/storage overhead for the event log — costs that are only justified by real scaling, performance, or auditability needs, not by a simple CRUD workload
CQRS and Event Sourcing can only be implemented on top of Kafka, which would be excessive infrastructure for an internal tool
Event Sourcing is fundamentally incompatible with relational databases, forcing an unwanted migration to NoSQL
CQRS mandates that the write and read models always share an identical schema, which defeats the purpose of adopting it
explanation: Both patterns are explicitly framed as tradeoffs, not universal upgrades: CQRS forces you to maintain and synchronize two models, and Event Sourcing forces you to manage replay cost, schema evolution, and ever-growing storage. For a low-complexity CRUD domain with no scaling pressure, that overhead has no offsetting benefit, which is precisely the scenario both sections call out as the biggest misuse of these patterns.
